articleTitle: A model for HF spectral occupancy
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: A record of HF occupancy has been made over a five-year period, and the paper describes an attempt to model some of the experimental results.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A wideband HF interference and noise model based on measured data
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Describes the first results of a high-resolution, wide-bandwidth North American HF band interference measurements program in terms of the correspondence of these results with a model for the interference derived from earlier European measurements. The preliminary conclusion is that the model is valid. The interference-dominated portion of the frequency distribution is approximately linear on a log-log plot which relates the fraction of the resolution cells occupied with interference at a power level to that power level.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Use of oblique-incidence-sounders in HF frequency management
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Examines the current status of OIS schemes for application in the management of frequencies in an HF system or complex of systems. Certain efforts are now underway to assess this approach to HF resource management in general and an understanding as to the direction of these programs is outlined. The authors indicate the NRL efforts in this context. Finally they provide a view as to the future of OIS in HF communications and surveillance areas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New HF spectrum occupancy measurements in Southern England
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Selected measurements of the HF fixed service bands are being carried out at a field site in southern England near the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory as part of a programme of ongoing study. This paper presents recent sample results of amplitude probability distributions (APDs) and unoccupied channel duration statistics using a single vertical whip (omnidirectional) receiving antenna and a filled array beamed either to the N or S. Data interpretation takes advantage of the extensive work carried out since the 1970s on the modelling of man-made interference and signal fading.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A performance study of the extended Kalman algorithm as a HF channel estimator
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: A study is made of the tracking and convergence properties of an extended Kalman (EK) algorithm as a high frequency (HF) channel estimator. This study uses the EK algorithm to adaptively estimate not only the time varying taps of the system but the parameters in the system model which generate the nonstationarity. This approach makes use of the a-priori knowledge of the HF channel to construct the extended Kalman algorithm for this system. Simulations are presented of the performance of the EK algorithm as a HF channel estimator for both white and coloured input signal conditions and are compared with the performance of the least mean square (LMS) and minimum variance Kalman (MVK) algorithms.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The wide-strip horizontal loop antenna (HLA): an effective solution for ground-wave interference to shortwave reception
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Horizontal loop antennas, called HLAs, improve overall signal quality on weak signals relative to the quality achieved using the standard telescoping whip which comes with most modern shortwave broadcast receivers. This article presents: (1) construction details for several versions of the HLA; and (2) operational instructions for use of the HLA with portable battery-operated shortwave receivers and with desktop receivers powered by AC.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New methods for signal separation
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Optimal reception of a source in the presence of sources of interference emitting, entirely or in part, in the same frequency band, can be obtained by modeling the radiation diagram of an antenna network, thus protecting radio communications against jamming. In the absence of multiple paths, this gain matching consists of a linear combination of signals received by the antenna sensors. One of the most generally used methods for this modeling is to separate the source signals. The sources can be discriminated by making use of the fundamental differences between the source signals: decorrelation; different powers; different spectra; and statistical independence. The two first points require traditional source signal separation methods. They consist of orthogonalizing sensor signals. These are substantially sub-optimal. The last two points, that is to say spectral differences and statistical independence, have led the authors to develop original separation methods. There are very nearly optimal.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Receiver design for HF ground-wave radar
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Ground-wave radars, operating in the HF band, are becoming increasingly popular for both the remote sensing of the sea surface and for the detection of ship targets well beyond the normal radar horizon. This paper details the requirements of the radar receiver and describes the gating system and the advantages of using digital signal processing techniques for the narrowband receiver functions. A coastal based pulse Doppler radar system as shown is considered. An omnidirectional antenna is used, on transmission, to 'floodlight' the sea surface. Directional information of the reflected target signal is then obtained using a wide aperture phased array antenna on reception. Effective target detection in the presence of sea clutter returns involves coherent integration of the echo, from a target, over a period of time which is in the order of 100's of seconds. A single narrow beam scanned in azimuth, as in microwave radars, would result in the introduction of an unacceptable time delay before returning to a given bearing. Thus the radar must use multiple beam synthesis from the phased array for target tracking and acquisition.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The performance of HF curtain antennas with irregular foregrounds
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The VRP of HF curtain arrays has traditionally been estimated by regarding the ground as a horizontal, reflecting plane. This approach has been shown to be inadequate for arrays with irregular foregrounds. A new model has been developed that calculates the current density induced by the array at small, regular intervals in the foreground. The values of current density are used to establish a set of discrete current elements, whose sum at various angles in the far field is used to calculate the effect of the foreground on the VRP. The results of the model are compared with experimental results obtained from tests at a BBC transmitting site.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An HF direction finding and null steering system employing a four element circular array
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Describes a small and potentially transportable HF (2-30 MHz) receiving and direction finding system which is also capable of null/beam steering. The system consists of a compact 4-element circular array, processor unit and a standard HF receiver. By using a null steering 'tree structure' within the processor unit, the system is capable of steering a null at an interfering signal and subsequently performing DF on a wanted co-channel signal. The objectives of the system have been met by utilising the properties of circular arrays consisting of wideband active elements, adaptive signal processing techniques and microprocessor control.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: HF data communication for extremely low SNR and high interference level
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: By using low data rates and both intelligent signal conception and digital signal processing (DSP) for estimation and detection, it is possible to realize new applications in the field of digital short wave communications (HF). For links with unknown interference level or low transmitter power, unmatched antennas and high path attenuation a special transmission principle was designed and realized. The authors see applications within emergency systems, for transmission of messages ensuring a reliable link establishment (e.g. frequency hopping) or for network control functions under severe interference conditions (intended or unintended). This low rate data modem is working in the baseband (300-3kHz) and can be operated with any HF SSB-transceiver. The use of a TMS 320 DSP architecture results in full real-time numerical signal processing and allows the implementation of detection algorithms based on FFT. The HF channel is investigated not only for detection of the desired signal but also for dealing with the interference situation, which is involved in the decoding process of the received data. By modifying parameters in the DSP software it is possible to obtain an adaptive mode where the signalling format tracks the quality of the channel.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An RTCE-assisted ARO transmission scheme: design & performance
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The authors provide an outline of the theory of the technique followed by a description of experiments to verify the method. Next, the design of an ARQ-based transmission system incorporating zero-crossing RTCE is described and its performance discussed. Finally, the application of higher-order zero-crossing analysis to RTCE and demodulation is considered. The dynamic range of the method is somewhat limited, but the system can be adaptively adjusted to make more effective use of this range by altering the length of the blocks over which analysis is carried out.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An anomalous effect in HF curtain arrays
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Discusses an effect which was discovered during the re-engineering of one of the BBC's HF transmitting sites. During the commissioning of the first array (a wideband, four-stack array) an effect was noted which gave rise to reflection coefficients of greater than unity in two of the stacks. This, if the array had been operated without any modifications, would have led to breakdown. Similar problems were observed in arrays which were subsequently erected by antenna contractors. It was found that by changing the feeder lengths it was possible to avoid (but not eliminate) the problem.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Software ionospheric channel simulator
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The ionospheric channel simulator described has been developed with the objective of evaluating HF modem performance either in fixed frequency or in frequency hopping mode. The simulator processes sampled data from complex signals generated by two kinds of sources: modem simulators; and hardware modems (an interface exists that performs the analog to digital conversion and generates the Q component of the complex signal). The following perturbations affecting HF transmissions have been taken into account: ionospheric propagation (Watterson Model); atmospheric noise; and interferences and jammers. In addition some effects of the transmitter-receiver (band-pass filtering, AGC) are included in the simulation. The software has been integrated on an array processor AP120B from FPS and a Vax 785 computer from DEC.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Ionospheric modelling based on oblique chirp-sounders
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Classical ionospheric HF propagation forecasts seem to result in significant differences compared with oblique chirp-plots. The Belgian Ministry of Foreign Affairs uses a centralized HF radio communications system for diplomatic purposes. Chirp-sounders are used to evaluate different main radiopaths before the radio transmissions take place and to correct (and improve) the maximum frequency forecast. The result for the path Brussels-Athens was analyzed during the months of June, July, August and September 1986 from the chirp-sounder-receiver. The results of the first test-month were used to adapt, from a popular algorithm, some parameters giving the MUF value.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Adaptive control and channel encoding in an automatic HF communication system
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The HF region of the radio spectrum is normally regarded as being unsuitable for reliable 24-hour communications due to time and spatial variability which can affect the availability and reliability of channels. The main parameters of concern are the variation in maximum and lowest usable frequencies, maximum data rate achievable, and the fading/interference structure at any time. Traditional approaches to overcoming the above variability in the channel can be grouped into three main categories, each having its own problems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rate 2/3 coded nonuniform phase/frequency modulation
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The authors propose the coded nonuniform FSK/PSK modulation technique to achieve further improvement of the performance over coded FSK/PSK system. They focus on a rate R=2/3 nonuniform coded 2-FSK/4-PSK modulations. The behavior of the free Euclidean distance is considered by varying the modulation index and three rotation angles which determine the nonuniform signal constellations. They also consider the effect of encoder structure and mapping method on the free Euclidean distance of nonuniform coded 2-FSK/4-PSK. The asymptotic performance gains due to coding and nonuniform constellation are evaluated in terms of the free Euclidean distance of the trellis. It is shown that at given modulation index the free Euclidean distance can be maximized by selecting the nonuniform signal constellations and the mapping method appropriately without increasing average or peak power or changing the bandwidth constraints imposed on the system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Numerical modelling and design of loaded broadband wire antennas
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: By making use of a sophisticated method of moments coded the performance of two published travelling wave wire antennas was analysed. An improved antenna, based on those concepts, was developed and considerable insight was gained into the criteria governing the operation of such antennas. Finally, a graphical technique was presented for the analysis and design of feedpoint-loaded antennas. This procedure enables optimum performance to be obtained from a clearly compromised antenna.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Real time HF channel evaluation and 8-ary FSK signaling for adaptive communications
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Modern HF radio communication requires operational simplicity and high reliability. However, continually changing ionospheric conditions make operations difficult, even by an experienced operator. The advent of adaptive technology has allowed systematic and automatic real-time evaluation of HF paths, and automatic link establishment. The Harris RF-7110 autolink adaptive controller is an example of state-of-the-art adaptive equipment, combining automatic link establishment and automatic link quality analysis (LQA). The authors show the autolink paired with the RT-1446/URC 100 watt transceiver, forming the RF-7100-04 adaptive communication system. Significant research and development has been completed which will enhance the next generation of the autolink controller by including 8-ary FSK (frequency shift keying) signaling and advanced link quality analysis (ALQA) techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: HF digital voice terminal
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The authors have developed a digital voice terminal which combines a modem and codec. It has proved successful for HF communication in the field. The digital voice terminal is composed of a voice codec, a modem, an interface circuit, and a power supply unit. The frequency division multiplexed and differential quadriphase shift keying (FDM-DQPSK) modem has a modulation rate of up to 2400 bps. The codec is a channel vocoder. The terminal is described with emphasis on the modulation/demodulation method, the coding/decoding system and the system configuration of the terminal.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experimental study of a modulation scheme for embedding data in DSB-AM
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Methods of embedding data in conventional DSB-AM signals are of interest in a number of applications including radiodata services for HF sound broadcasting. The data signals carry information which can be used by specially equipped receivers for various display and control functions such as automatic retuning when the transmission frequency is changed. In the case of DSB-AM, frequency modulation of the carrier in addition to the usual envelope modulation can provide a data channel but unless the data rate is very small the modulated signal is likely to exceed its allocated bandwidth. Zero-synchronous modulation (ZSM) is a spectrally-efficient combined AM/FM scheme proposed by Lockhart and Al-Jalili (1982) which permits data to be embedded in DSB-AM without significantly increasing the bandwidth or distorting the envelope. An experimental transmitter/receiver system constructed to study the practical performance of ZSM is described and some results presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: 2.4 kbit/s adaptive serial modems for HF skywave paths
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: It is only recently that the processing power required by adaptive modems of this type has been available from digital signal processors (DSPs) suitable for use in modems. This is especially true in the case of a channel estimating modem of the type described, where a near-maximum likelihood detector (NMLD) is employed. Prototype 2.4 kbit/s modems have been developed with the aim of achieving the best possible performance on HF skywave paths subject to multipath, fast fading and interference. Of particular interest are paths subject to high auroral absorption effects, where fade rates of 5 to 10 Hz are not uncommon. The channel estimator plus near-maximum likelihood detector system proposed and developed by Clark, Asghar and McVerry (1981) was chosen as the structure best able to cope with fast fading conditions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Phase delay compensation in HF Cartesian-loop transmitters
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Radio transmitters intended for use with amplitude modulation, including single side-band, require a linear power amplifier to raise the power of the modulated signal to that necessary for transmission. In this amplification process lies a problem: that of obtaining good spectral purity of the output signal whilst maintaining a reasonable power conversion efficiency. This paper describes briefly an HF Cartesian-loop transmitter, and then gives details of the phase delay compensation scheme developed to maintain stable operation of the feedback loops over the entire HF band.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Weekly and daily radioelectric propagation conditions forecasting in the Tahiti region
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Long term radioelectric propagation conditions forecasting is necessary to establish radioelectric links (antennas, frequencies, power and hours working determination). It gives the evolution of the conditions of propagation for a given probability. The day to day variation of the critical frequency of the F2 layer (foF2), one of the most important characteristics, presents a large variation in comparison with the median. It takes into account neither the fine evolution of both solar and magnetic activity nor ionospheric storms. Therefore it is necessary to establish weekly and daily forecasting. The purpose of this paper is to present a statistical model of foF2 above Tahiti which permits one to calculate the foF2 values a function of both solar and magnetic activity on a week or a day base.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic HF signal classification
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Describes an automatic real-time HF signal classifier which has been implemented at extremely low cost with standard hardware. The classifier allows automatic recognition of the following types of received signals: unmodulated carrier, double sideband amplitude modulation (AM), single sideband voice modulation (SSB), binary FSK, multichannel FSK, binary ASK and noise. Those are the basic emissions in the HF band.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Launching of HF surface waves
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: A technique for obtaining approximately 3 dB improvement in HF signal strength at ground level over that obtained from a vertically polarised dipole has been described. This use of inductive loading has been shown to be relatively broadband. The work described in this paper forms part of an ongoing programme of research for communication and radar applications for the efficient utilisation of HF antennas, which has particular reference to coastal sites. At such sites the antenna must be placed with the driven elements some distance back from the tide-line, and the intervening ground is often overlaid by a wire grid screen. The principles described shows that by adding a second 'layer' to the ground, an enhancement in the radiated field relative to the perfect conductor is possible. Future tests will involve the use of shipborne measurements with the ground loading turned round so as to direct radiation over the sea rather than over the land.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: HF ground-wave radar; theory and practice
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: High speed digital signal processing, automatic radar management, target extraction and real time display are some of the salient features of recent, commercially available modern HF radar. This paper is an appraisal of the theoretical background involved in a ground-wave HF radar design.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The localization technique for the experimental HF skywave radar
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The authors have put forward a method to calculate the ground distance of fixed discrete scatterers see Chinese J. Space Science, vol.7, no.1, p.59, 1987. The present paper gives a method for locating moving targets, based on the above method. The only parameters needed are the minimum time delay curve, the echo time delays and the Doppler frequencies of the moving object. The first is provided by a sweep frequency backscatter sounder at the radar site and the others by the HF radar. There is no need to know the ionospheric data at the middle point of the path. It is the object of this paper to present details of the equipment used in these experiments, the theory of the method and results of the analysis of the radical tracks of targets.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The design and simulation of an adaptive HF data network
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The availability of agile, remotely controllable HF equipment has been exploited in the design of an HF data network which will provide communications between some 80 locations in a full deployment. Each station will be software controlled so that network management, frequency management and link management will be handled automatically without operator intervention. This represents a major improvement in HF systems which have traditionally relied on the skills of experienced operators to achieve adequate performance. The network architecture will be outlined with a high level description of the network management, frequency management and link management subsystems. Then a traffic simulation model is described which has been a valuable tool in the design of the network and, more importantly, will be an essential element in network acceptance testing.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An interactive HF computer link
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Since the beginning of this century ionospheric propagation (HF) has been an important medium of radio communications. It has supported commercial telegraphy, telex traffic and military communications. Although it is a communication channel with high data corruption, the low cost of an HF system compared to the satellite for a small to medium number of users, the lower vulnerability in military applications, and the facility to follow the state of the art more frequently due to lower sophistication than the satellite schemes, make it an interesting alternative for communication. However, little consideration has been shown in the use of this medium for computer communications. The need for communications of this type is becoming clear. The authors discuss the utilisation of an HF link as a medium supporting a remote interactive terminal-computer communication.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Enhancement of remote sensing capability of HF skywave radar by correcting the signal for frequency modulations
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Ionospherically propagated signals are frequently affected by short-term phase-path variations degrading the remote sensing capabilities of HF skywave radar, in particular for sea state applications. The authors have proposed a method to correct the phase of the signal reflected by the ionosphere and backscattered by the sea surface, based on the derivation of an estimator of the frequency modulation affecting the wave after the double ionospheric transit. This signal processing method has been applied to a large data set and, in the present paper, they study the dependence of the equivalent width of the sea-scatter Bragg line on the coherent integration time. They show that the correction of the phase allows the use of longer coherent integration times and thus improves the detection capabilities of HF radar for targets in sea clutter.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Space diversity reception in meteor burst communications system
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Presents some early results from a dual investigation of the data both in terms of cross-correlation coefficients and in terms of an assessment of the available duty cycle with and without spatial diversity. This study has not yet revealed whether space diversity provides a significant increase in performance and further study is necessary before a definitive statement can be made.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An adaptive HF system and its computerized performance evaluation
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Presents the principal requirements from a modern adaptive HF communication system, the basic design concepts of the implemented system which successfully answers these requirements, the accompanying field trial methodology and briefly, some of the field trials results. The basic lesson learned from the implementation and the field trials of the described system is that a modern HF communication system can fulfil the current and future requirements of C3I systems only if it glues together a number of technical features including self-healing architecture, automatic digital operation, real time, adaptive frequency management, HF oriented error detection and correction codes and communication protocols. ALE, LQA and simple and efficient man-machine interfaces. A mandatory phase is developing such systems is the field trials which should be performed with computer aid, using appropriate methodology and tools.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A modular frequency management facility with application at HF
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Frequency management techniques are playing an increasingly important role in the design and implementation of the new generation of tactical and strategic HF communications systems. The increasing demand for high quality data links and spread spectrum capability has established automated frequency management as a necessity rather than just a convenience. The authors outline the purpose of frequency management, the major components of a particular frequency management facility developed in Australia, and two projects to which this facility has been applied. They conclude with a statement of the efficacy of frequency management and likely future directions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Digital HF modem performance measurements using HF link simulators
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: One testing technique is that of using channel simulators which can provide identical statistical stress on the modems under test. A recommended set of tests, which include testing with simulated interference conditions, has been included as Annex B in the proposed NATO Standard 4285. Although not perfect, this set of tests is believed to be a reasonable compromise between required test time and modem characterization. If one examines this section of the Standard, however, he discovers that some of the recommended tests (those involving bit error rate vs. average signal-to-noise ratio) require what might be considered an unreasonable time to conduct. The authors discuss the basis of those time recommendations and some of the logical consequences of them.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Mutual coupling and phase control on large HF arrays
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: When using a large phase array in order to carry out active sensing or direction finding in the HF band, various effects act on the processing of the array signals. Some are related to the design of the array and can be corrected (insufficient knowledge of the sensor positions, lack of antennas reproducibility). Others affect the shape of the wavefront onto the array due either to propagation internal to the antenna (VSWR) or to external propagation (multipaths, ionospheric channel fluctuations, mutual coupling between elements).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A wideband transportable antenna for NVIS links
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Since the advent of improved satellite and cable services, HF radio is increasingly being used to provide short and medium distance communications, especially between mobile or transportable stations. The propagation characteristics for these shorter links require the use of correctly chosen frequencies and antennas which radiate at the angle of elevation which is necessary. It is clear from the parameters which are currently being specified for antennas for these links, that engineers who are specifying equipment are not very familiar with the exact characteristics which are needed. It is the objective of this paper to examine the operational requirements and to determine the characteristics which suitable antennas must provide. A number of simple antenna designs are then reviewed for their suitability for use is lightweight transportable systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Single-tone HF data transmission with 2.4 kbps and 4.8 kbps
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: In the past few years powerful single-tone modems for data transmission via HF radio links became realizable. These single-tone modems overcome many of the shortcomings of conventional parallel tone-type modems, but it is very important to apply proper designed signal processing algorithms and coding schemes to cope with the disturbing effects on HF radio channels, i.e. with time-varying multipath propagation and strong additive interference. A modem for 2.4 kbps using 4 PSK, adaptive decision feedback equalization (DFE) and Reed-Solomon (RS) coding is dealt with. Some features of 4.8 kbps algorithms using 16 PSK trellis coding and Viterbi algorithm (VA) equalization/decoding are also described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A computer aided design tool for collocated HF links
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: There have been many programs and techniques developed to deal with the cosite EMI problem. Previous programs have evolved from semimanual to highly automated techniques. However the EMI problem has grown to such an extent on today's ships that system design and analysis requires computer aided tools. COEDS (communication engineering design system) is one of the tools that has been developed to aid in the topside design and interference analysis problem.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An adaptive digital receiver for HF communication
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The fading characteristics of the HF channel make communication over this channel difficult, even at moderate data rates. An adaptive receiver for data detection and adaptive optimization to the channel parameters is presented. The channel tracking is performed during the training sequence as well as during the detected data sequence. The receiver is fast converging, therefore suitable for frequency hopping. The paper presents an improved version of the adaptive receiver, compared to the version presented by Perl, Shpigel and Reichman (see IEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communication, vol.SAC-5, no.2, p.304, 1987). The improvement is in the required computational complexity without loss in performance. The performance obtained on simulated HF channels and the computational complexity are presented, via comparisons with previously published results.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Planning and operation of an HF broadcast relay station
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: International short wave broadcasting has expanded on a worldwide scale and in order to maintain a UK presence in this field of broadcasting the BBC has expanded and improved its transmission facilities to meet the increased competition that exists in the HF broadcast spectrum. This has been achieved within the UK by a progressive replacement of old 100kW HF transmitters by modern high efficiency high power 500kW transmitters. Overseas, the building of strategically positioned HF relay stations complements the UK bases so that today the BBC operates 5 stations within the UK and 8 overseas stations. The most recent addition to these relay bases is that at Hong Kong which was officially opened on September 27th 1987. The authors describe the need for such a station, aspects associated with the planning and construction and operational considerations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of DSP techniques in HF radio receiver design
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: A typical receiver has a two or three stage superheterodyne structure to achieve the very high degree of discrimination against out of band signals necessary to operate in what has become a very crowded part of the radio spectrum. Recent advances in digital signal processing technology now offer the possibility of implementing many of the signal processing functions digitally. This paper examines the performance requirements necessary for operation in the HF band and the manner in which these are met by purely analogue receivers. It then examines the performance requirements for a digital receiver, A-D conversion techniques and digital implementation of the traditional receiver functions of channel filtering, SSB separation, AGC and demodulation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Low distortion RF component technology development
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: A wideband communication system architecture is being developed for the US Navy in the high frequency (HF), 2 to 30 MHz range. The goals for the architecture provide essentially instantaneous access to the entire HF spectrum for all exciters and receivers while maintaining the sensitivity and distortion performance of the best of conventional systems. The Westinghouse Electric Corporation designed and built four low power four port hybrid combiner/dividers, four low power four input single output hybrid combiner/dividers, two high power four port combiner/dividers, four each low power 7 dB and 14 dB directional couplers, and two high power 20 dB directional couplers for use in the implementation of feedforward technology. This paper briefly reviews the approach used to meet the performance requirements by first discussing the initial investigations into available ferrous materials, then presenting three design techniques used to fulfill the requirements, and finally, focusing on the performance of a representative sample of the components delivered by Westinghouse to the Navy.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Adaptive data link protocols: design and performance over automated HF skywave links
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: HF today offers increased reliability on account of equipment improvements and the application of embedded processing, facilitating network frequency and link management. This has lead to a resurgence of interest in its use for data communications where the emphasis is on achieving high integrity without sacrificing throughput. Powerful techniques are needed to achieve these goals in the hostile HF medium with its inherent channel capacity variations and where spectral efficiency considerations preclude the use of highly redundant coding (and overheads) and limit the amount of repetition which can be tolerated. The key concept pervading modern HF systems is adaption, and this needs to be included in the design of data link protocols. In the protocol described throughput is varied in response to changes in channel condition (both interference and propagation) while maintaining consistent high integrity. Note that the protocol is more than just a means of providing an error free data stream; it is an integral part of the management of modern networks covering control, as well as message functions. The authors discuss the design aspects of new selective ARQ data link protocols and shows the results of extensive live trials over an HF test-bed facility.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Soft decoding of recorded HF data
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: In the search for good error control codes with known decoding algorithms, for the frequency hopping HF channel, the authors have studied how channel measurement information can improve the error-correcting capability of the code. They show the performance of some well-known error-correcting codes when used on the HF channel together with channel measurement information. A frequency hopping system working at HF has been built and tested. The system is built as an experimental system to investigate the various problems one has to deal with when using spread-spectrum coding. The intention is to demonstrate the efficiency with this kind of system compared to other systems in a hostile jamming environment. Based on data recorded from the HF system they have implemented two types of soft decoding algorithms in software and simulated their performances. The two decoding algorithms are the Blokh-Zyablov algorithm and the Chase algorithm.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An experimental HF ground wave radar
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The main tasks for the experimental station described were to establish, for future operational consideration, consistency of aircraft detection, to demonstrate continuous radar cover in time and in space and that it would be possible to deploy with reasonable logistic HF support. It should confirm the parameters of the HF radar equation, confirm the existence of reliable propagation paths close to the sea and show that the inevitable sea clutter could readily be filtered out; ionospheric clutter returns should not present intractable problems. The HF radar cross sections of various targets should prove large enough to enable long range detections, and most importantly the radar should be acceptable as a new user of this portion of the spectrum. Main equipment items should be procurable without extensive development, which implies that the special demands of radar, compared with communications, should be realisable by modification of existing communication, transmitters and receivers. It was to be demonstrated that with recent advances in digital data processors offering continuous throughput of some 10 million Floating Point operations per second, real time operation of the radar would be possible.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Real time large scale modelisation of the ionosphere with back scatter sounding-news results
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Describes the development of a simple and direct method of real time inversion of the back scatter ionogram. The originality of the method lies in a double modelisation: that of the electron density profile, and that of the backscatter ionogram. This procedure offers the advantage of reducing each model to a few number of parameters among them it is possible to establish numerical relations. In practice the number of parameters describing the ionogram model is always smaller than the number of parameters describing the electron density profile, so the inversion is only possible if complementary data are available. The authors have shown that this can be done by using fixed frequency variable azimuth backscatter soundings (PPI), which allows us to find the bearing of horizontal gradients. The inversion method which has been developed ensures good stability of the solution.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: BLOSSOM-a technical description of the RAE meteor burst communications system
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Presents a technical description of the BLOSSOM (beyond line of sight signalling over meteors) MBC system as at March 1986. The BLOSSOM system can be split up into three main parts. Firstly, the RF subsystem, built by RAE, comprising all the RF equipment including antennas, RF converters, transmitter, relays, switches and protection circuitry. Secondly, the control subsystem, built by PRRML, comprising the control units, together with the modem which is itself internal to the control unit. The third subsystem is the computer, plotter, and the BLOSSOM program which controls the equipment and experiments. In addition, an Omega navigation system locked clock is provided for accurate system timing. The RF equipment was designed to cope with four possible operating frequencies at approximately 36, 46, 70 and 71 MHz.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Ionospheric probing with an HF radar
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The JINDALEE radar has been designed primarily for extended coverage air defence surveillance of Australia's northern coastline. It achieves its long-range over-the-horizon (OTH) capability by employing ionospheric reflection; therefore ionospheric information is obtained as a by-product of radar operations. This paper describes some radar results concerning TID's (travelling ionospheric disturbances), effects of the dawn terminator passage, geographic variations of ionization density and meteor backscatter. Examples are given of geographic variations and dynamic behaviour of the measured ionospheric parameters. In addition, the results obtained from the observations of meteor trail backscatter are summarised.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Practical real time frequency management for automated HF networks
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: A frequency management system for an automatic HF network is described. MUF updates are calculated automatically with 99% reliability without the need for dedicated, specialist equipment. The process also allows disturbances to be identified and utilised if appropriate. Channel selection is achieved in such a way as to minimise interference and maximise reliability. The chosen channel is monitored throughout the passing of the message in order to allow rapid response to changing conditions. The techniques have been tested over a 132 km link with encouraging results. They are being incorporated into a network of 80 stations which will shortly be undergoing acceptance tests.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modelling in the HF network design process
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Modelling can play a significant role in the design process by providing the ability to trade off a wide range of parameters in a cost effective and well controlled manner. The author presents an example of how modelling has been used to assist the design specification of an HF radio network and to predict its performance under a wide range of conditions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Portable unidirectional HF receiving aerial for reducing co-channel multihop sky-wave interference
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Fortunately, the great strength of shortwave broadcasts makes physically-small designs feasible. This article describes a compact aerial suitable for rejecting sky-wave signals and having a cardioidal pattern. It is intended to be used right beside a receiver, either indoors or out, and to have dimensions comparable with, or smaller than, the whips in common use.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Performance of the receivers of trellis-coded data signals transmitted through HF channels
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Shows the results of investigation by computer simulation of several receiver structures for trellis-coded signals transmitted through an HF radio channel. It is well known that application of Ungerboeck codes jointly with PSK or QAM modulation and the soft-decision Viterbi algorithm results in 2-6 dB asymptotic gain depending on the applied code. However, it is worth investigating the effective gain over uncoded systems when deep selective fades and ISI occur and signal-to-noise ratio is low or moderate, as in HF channels.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Short range communication systems, design and operation at very high latitudes
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Illustrates high latitude effects with vertical incidence ionograms recorded in north-east Greenland (80 degrees N, 20 degrees W) during the operation of a HF network for short range communication, 0-600 km in a mountainous area in July 1980. The network comprised two master stations, approximately 20 field stations, three helicopters and a fixed wing aircraft. The propagation mode for the network was exclusively ionospheric reflections, as even very short distances, of 10-30 km, spanned from valley to valley, eliminating ground wave propagation. The ionogram data are compared to ionospheric characteristics published by CCIR, and the usefulness of these are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Antenna arrays of the CNET backscatter HF radar
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: An antenna system for an ionospheric backscatter sounder is being installed by CNET at Lannion. This system has been designed to sweep the main beam in azimuth and elevation over a wide range of frequencies (6-30 MHz), while providing the most constant narrow-beam possible. Towards this aim the authors have proposed a method of beam shaping based on a physical approach. The effects of phase and amplitude dispersion associated with the elements making up the backscatter sounder on the performance of this new method are evaluated by simulation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Real-time frequency selection and HF spectrum monitor
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Early in the 1980s, a real-time frequency selecting system, abbreviated to RTFSS, was developed in China and successfully used in communication. Equipped with a spectrum monitor, the system can select frequency for both directions. This system can automatically establish an HF link in the best channel. Several methods of data processing are improved based upon the CURTS system, therefore the reliability of predicting optimal frequency has greatly been enhanced. The improved data processing and applied effects are emphasized.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The active receiving antenna, an appropriate element for HF-radio reception
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: New techniques of highly linear and low noise amplifier circuits provide extremely broadband active antennas and antenna couplers for application in HF-VHF receiving systems. The undesired frequency dependence of the performance of antennas mounted on masts can be effectively suppressed by the use of small active loop antennas. By multiple use of the diversity-antennas in combination with appropriate circuit devices the decoupling from the mast can also be obtained with active electric dipoles. Therefore antennas of this kind being mounted upon masts of appropriate heights are highly qualified elements for application in antenna arrays.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An HF radio link processor with adaptive frequency management
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The reliability of modern HF-communication systems is essentially influenced by the effectiveness of the frequency management. The important functions are: selection of momentary best frequency from a frequency pool with dependence of transmission parameters; control of transmission quality; and change of frequency as a reaction to interference. Functions like these can be handled in a more effective way by fast processors with proper designed transmission protocols. The key for optimizing the procedures is the combination of different methods which are available for channel analysis. The evaluation of transmission characteristics in real time (real time channel evaluation), ionospheric predictions and link statistics are the basis for a proper automatic selection of frequencies in any situation within a radio network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Interference tests on HF modems
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Proposes a series of laboratory tests, based on generic types of interference, which could be used to provide reference data for the comparison of alternative modem designs. The rationale for the selected set of tests is described. These measurements were originally developed to permit the qualitative evaluation of medium speed HF data modems, operating at information rates of 1200 and 2400 bits/second. To illustrate the test procedures, the results obtained from measurements on two types of medium-speed modems are presented. These results show that the tests provide a useful indication of the modems' sensitivity to interference.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A computer program to calculate the coverage and compatibility of HF broadcasts in the presence of noise and interference
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The principle of ionospheric prediction methods is to analyse the propagation conditions at several discrete points along the great-circle path between two given terminals. As the main results the highest and lowest usable frequencies or the field strengths at specified frequencies are obtained. These results are strictly valid only at the receiving point or its immediate neighbourhood and are therefore best suited for point-to-point transmission links. Contrary to this, the planning of HF broadcast services requires the knowledge of fieldstrength coverages of usually far extended areas within which the propagation conditions as well as the interference situation may change rather rapidly. In the past computations for this purpose were restricted to some few representative paths due to the excessive computation times. With the appearance of fast prediction programs it is now possible not only to use algorithms for area covering calculations but also to take interference computations into account.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Direction finding using a wide aperture circular array with minimum antenna elements
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Discusses the development of an equipment which will measure azimuth and elevation bearing angles, will operate on good and poor DF sites and be suitable for use in either transportable or fixed roles. Operation on poor DF sites, with a number of nearby signal reflections, and operation with high elevation angle sky-wave signals means that a wide aperture system should be used. However, the need for transportability and rapid deployment implies that the number of elements in the antenna array should be reduced to a minimum. This paper describes the system which has been developed and gives the theoretical performance and practical results obtained using the system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simplified HF communications station using an adaptive processor
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The 1980s has seen a resurgence in interest in the HF spectrum and its potential for reliable data communications. Considerable progress has been made in the use of real-time channel evaluation (RTCE), automated frequency management, and compact ionospheric prediction programs. The availability of powerful, reasonably priced computers and the widespread provision of remote control facilities on communications equipment in recent years has made possible the design of highly automated HF networks embodying RTCE and frequency management to give tangible benefits to the end user. The author describes the architecture of a message handling station designed as part of such a network. Consideration of the principal design constraints is followed by a description of the equipment, focussing on the HF adaptive processor at the heart of the station. The author finally lists some of the benefits reaped from the new architecture.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Receiving system linearity requirements for HF radar
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: In designing an HF radar receiving system it is highly desirable that the system sensitivity should be limited by external noise, rather than by internal noise or nonlinearities within the receiving system. Sources of internal noise may be suppressed by preceding stages of active gain, provided that the antenna design ensures an adequate available ratio of external/internal noise. The purpose of this paper is to establish design criteria for the effective removal of nonlinear effects associated with the front-end of such a receiving system. The objectives of this paper are thus: (i) to obtain a quantitative measure of radar performance degradation due intermodulation distortion, (ii) to compare the result obtained in (i) with a previously obtained measure relating to cross-modulation in order to decide which mechanism is the more potent and consequently which should be used in specifying the so called out-of-band third order intercept point; (iii) to note the influence of directive antenna gain in relation to the above; and (iv) to present experimental data based on the above theory.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A null-steering adaptive array processor for voiceband HF links
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: An alternative to interference avoidance is interference cancellation with null steering adaptive arrays. Although this approach does demand additional antennas and receivers, it allows use of the entire channel bandwidth at occupied frequencies, provided the number of interfering signals is less than the number of array elements. A general purpose, null steering, adaptive array processor (AAP) for voiceband HF channels is currently under company-funded development at Rockwell International, Collins Defense Communications. It is expected that by adding this applique to existing, conventional (nonhopping) HF communication systems, significant performance improvements will be available through interference rejection.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analysis of shipboard HF antennas with PDMPH2 computer code
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The analysis of some shipboard HF antennas is quite complicated. This contribution shows the numerical and experimental results obtained for the rather realistic configuration formed by a twin fan antenna and a monopole centered on the top of a conducting box, both antennas being on an infinite conducting ground plane. Calculations and measurements are in very good agreement. The computer code PDMPH2 (wire modelling) has been used. The experiments have been performed in an anechoic chamber.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Real time 800 bits/s linear predictive vocoder for HF communications
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Describes both simulation and real-time implementation of an 800 bits/s vector quantization LPC vocoder. Vector quantization requires a training algorithm to design efficient codebooks of LP filters (in other words, codebooks that fit the distribution of the input vectors). It also requires a fast nearest neighbour search algorithm for real time encoding of the LP filters. These algorithms are summarized. The hardware configuration is described. It consists mainly of a TMS 32010 processor board and of a memory board. The speech quality and intelligibility at 800 bits/s have been subjectively evaluated with informal listening tests and Diagnostic Rhyme Tests performance results are presented. The performances of this vocoder in the case of HF communications under degraded conditions is briefly evaluated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ARTAC-an automatic adaptive HF radio system in field tests
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: Discusses how in an automatic, adaptive HF system with error correction, RF power output levels around 400W will provide good results. To enhance the reliability and throughput of the link, especially over the shorter distances, the allocated frequencies should include the 'odd' bands (the high bands that were not listed as useable in the traditional predictions). Further studies of sporadic E reflections will be required. The present analysis of existing test plots shows that the full potential of these reflections has not been utilized. The analysis of the test results are notable in another respect. The residual character error-rate is <10-6 for the short links, and approximately=10-5 for the longer. This difference indicates that there is room for further investigation and improvements in the error-correcting methods or algorithms.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experimental comparisons of sky wave DF algorithms using a small circular array of loop antennas
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: A large quantity of array responses to skywave signals has been recorded by an automated data acquisition system and has been processed using several fundamentally different algorithms for estimating azimuth angle of arrival. The skywave signals incident on the array were generated by a controlled transmitter positioned at ranges varying from 278 to 1379 km, and operating at frequencies from 2 to 15 MHz. The data were processed to compare the experimental performance of a synthesized spinning spaced loop system, a synthesized system of magnetic dipoles and symmetric magnetic quadrupoles, and a form of sum-and-difference mode DF. To provide comparative results from a system having well understood polarization error, the data were also processed with a conventional simple loop DF algorithm.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: HF data message and facsimile terminal system
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The data terminal (HF-Maxi terminal) is an outcome of the research and development done by CRC. The first generation of the HF message terminal developed by CRC (HF-Mini terminal) used a simple selective ARQ protocol for data transmission reference. Alternate techniques were investigated to improve the ARQ protocol for the second generation of a HF packet radio system by utilizing the soft decision information received in a block with errors in subsequent receptions to improve throughput of the system. The HF-Maxi terminal system was designed built and extensively tested over sky wave paths to prove the viability of transmitting large data files at high speeds through HF radio channels. The system has facilities to input text, data and facsimile images for transmission.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Numerical modelling of the ship antennas array
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: The author presents a numerical method of ship antenna array analysis. The influence of the ship transmitter antenna on the ship receiver antenna is described. The linear antenna, especially the monopole antenna, is the main type of the ship antenna array. The numerical model is applied using the thin-wire model of the linear antenna array. The theoretical results have been verified by experiments.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A method of real-time channel evaluation in adaptive HF systems
publicationTitle: 1988 Fourth International Conference on HF Radio Systems and Techniques
abstract: A simple and cost effective channel evaluation method, suitable for application to an adaptive HF system, is proposed. The method is based on a modification of a well known Gooding's pseudo error monitoring scheme. A theoretical and experimental research was carried on to find the trade-off between the confidence level of channel quality estimation and length of measurement interval. Some results of this research are presented, together with a description of the method.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
